title: Generative Agents: Interactive Simulacra of Human Behavior
problem: Creating interactive artificial societies and computational agents that can simulate believable human behavior over long time horizons while maintaining memory, planning, and coherence.
method: An agent architecture combining large language models with a memory stream (recording experiences), retrieval mechanisms (evaluating recency, importance, and relevance), periodic reflection (synthesizing higher-level inferences), and hierarchical planning.
datasets: Smallville sandbox environment (The Sims-inspired town with 25 agents)
key_results: The full generative agent architecture achieved the highest believability rating (TrueSkill mean 29.89) compared to ablated versions and human crowdworkers.

Emergent social behaviors were observed, including information diffusion (e.g., Sam's mayoral candidacy spreading from 4% to 32% of agents), relationship formation (network density increased from 0.167 to 0.74), and coordination (agents organizing and attending a Valentine's Day party from a single user seed).
limitations: Retrieval challenges and hallucinations when managing large memory streams.
Errors in understanding physical norms and constraints of locations (e.g., single-person bathrooms or closed stores).
Instruction tuning side effects causing agents to be overly formal and excessively cooperative/polite.
future_work: Enhancing the retrieval module and fine-tuning ranking functions for better relevance.
Improving computational performance and reducing token costs/latency to enhance real-time interactivity.
Observing agent behavior over longer timescales and establishing more rigorous performance benchmarks.
Improving underlying models for better value alignment and reduced biases for marginalized populations.
key_claims: Generative agents powered by the proposed architecture produce significantly more believable individual behavior than models without memory, planning, or reflection.
The architecture enables complex emergent social behaviors such as information diffusion, relationship formation, and coordination without hard-coded rules.
Reflection is critical for agents to synthesize experiences and make higher-level inferences when answering questions or making decisions.
references_cited: Stuart K Card, Thomas P Moran, and Allen Newell. 1980. The keystroke-level model for user performance time with interactive systems.
John Laird and Michael VanLent. 2001. Human-Level AI’s Killer Application: Interactive Computer Games.
Joon Sung Park, Lindsay Popowski, Carrie J. Cai, Meredith Ringel Morris, Percy Liang, and Michael S. Bernstein. 2022. Social Simulacra: Creating Populated Prototypes for Social Computing Systems.
